title: MNC IPO theme to stay in India, but investors will push for more disclosures, say top bankers- Moneycontrol.com
text:
My Alerts Go Ad-Free Follow us on: Global beer major Carlsberg has filed draft papers for $700 million IPO while Coca-Cola’s bottling arm and Pernod Ricard India are also eyeing domestic listings   September 15, 2026 / 15:03 IST             After a muted start to FY27, equity capital market deal activities in India across IPOs and block trades gradually picked up in June and July and finally exploded in August. So, what are the top trends and sectors to watch out for in the rest of the fiscal? Ranvir Davda, Co-Head, Investment Banking, HSBC India, and Jibi Jacob, MD & Head, Equity Capital Markets, Jefferies India, spoke to Moneycontrol's Ashwin Mohan to discuss all this and more. Both dealmakers believe the trend of MNC IPO’s will continue in India, but notwithstanding the valuation arbitrage factor, they highlight that investors will demand more disclosures and ask whether two key variables, revenues and costs, reside domestically or not. Edited Excerpts: What are the specific themes that institutional money has chased so far in FY27 when it comes to listings, block deals and QIPs? Can you stick your neck out and name the sectors that are witnessing genuine demand and why, versus those sectors that are merely riding sentiment? Ranvir Davda: I think India is amid a few secular themes and the first one that I can clearly call out is the industrials/manufacturing, auto components, Make in India, and export to the world theme. Across this group, which we refer to as “ industrials”, we have seen almost $4-$5 billion of primary IPOs and secondary blocks. Clearly, India is emerging as an export-oriented country, and the growth that we can offer with this sort of manufacturing in India-led growth is seeing strong interest. There are also lots of domestic funds and international funds that have these manufacturing themes. I think the second bucket is the energy transition and renewable play. You saw IPOs from the sector; you saw follow-ons from the sector getting done. As crude oil and market volatility play out, India must become self-independent. The pipeline also shows that there is more to come from this table. The third theme is the new economy linked to what we call the overall tech economy. But within that also, there are nuances of B2B, consumer tech and fintech. I think those three continue to dominate for at least this part, the secondary market volumes, because last year, in the month of November and December, you saw a lot of new economy IPOs coming from the likes of Groww, Lenskart, Meesho. Those issue had lock-up expiries coming through now, so they saw a lot of volume. Finally, financial services has always been a mainstay in Indian capital markets. Now within financial services, it could be savings or non-savings linked. I think we are seeing more ( action) on the non-savings linked category, like financial infrastructure, which is seeing a lot of interest from investors. That’s what's really driving primary market and blocks volume. Is the market signaling to issuer companies that IPOs where the primary component is more than secondary, are preferred or at least a combination of both components is vital? The idea being that later, one can monetize stake via blocks in a gradual manner which seems like a tried and tested model now. In fact blocks seem to be increasingly replacing QIPs as the preferred sell down route, plus they are cheaper and faster to execute. Jibi Jacob: Ashwin, I think the right way to look at this, and this is how the potential investors also look at it, is that are you should be raising sufficient primary capital which is required to run the business for 18 to 24 months. That has been our advice to clients as well. Raise enough primary capital for 18 to 24 months. And to top it up, have a secondary component built into it to make it a sizable deal for the global investors and larger domestic mutual funds to get a sizable allocation. So going in, yes, primary is most preferred. But you can see a lot of issuers who do not need primary capital to grow the business. They are self-funded or have enough capital or internal accruals to grow the business. In those cases, we have no qualms in telling them, why don't you do a completely secondary deal? So, I would say it's based on business to business. Wherever there is a need for capital, do raise. Otherwise, a completely 100 per cent secondary offering is possible. I don't think any of the buy side investors also blink an eye when there is a larger secondary offering. Hyundai Motors opened the MNC IPO floodgates in India with its record issue, followed by LG Electronics which shook the market with a 54x subscription. The likes of Orkla and Tenneco followed, Carlsberg filed its draft papers and now we have Coca-Cola’s bottling arm, Pernod Ricard and others in the pipeline. Does the solo swing factor for MNC IPO’s remain the India valuation arbitrage opportunity? Jibi Jacob: It is a combination of a couple of things, Ashwin. One is, obviously, the valuation arbitrage. Indian markets do provide a very high degree of multiple for the growth assets that these MNC players have in India. Secondly, a lot of them are also strategic in nature, wanting to be present and seen in India as a very serious player. But if you take a step back and just look at Indian capital markets, there are very tight capital controls that apply to all of us. There is an LRS regulatory framework where you can take out $250,000 US dollars in a year as an individual. And that is the cap that an Indian resident has without specific approval. So Indian savers can't really access the foreign-listed peers or issuers in a meaningful manner. Of course, Gift City has come in and all credit to government in terms of enabling it or channelizing these savings to some extent to the foreign markets. But overall, the mutual funds have a $7 billion cap, as you would know, of investing overseas. So if Indian savers can't reach there, what is the synthetic way for these issuers to tap into that? I would say MNC IPOs are also a result of the fact that you are now able to list your Indian subsidiaries and tap into the Indian savers. Ranvir Davda: We were part of the Hyundai IPO and it's public that we filed papers for the Sembcorp India IPO. When we as a global franchise are sitting in the boardrooms, either in Asia or in Europe, we clearly say that, yes, the valuation arbitrage is real, but a listing comes with its own set of responsibilities when you become a part of Indian capital markets. And that requires India-specific growth. It requires the same credible governance. It requires sole decision and joint decision making in India along with the parent management. It requires very good disclosures around related party transactions, around royalty payments. It requires the mutual fund investor to feel comfortable that they are able to see the value add coming from the parent, which is being utilized by the Indian listed company. Now, as you correctly said, this trend has really seen a lot of volume of companies come through. As this MNC theme and the cohort increases, I think investors will start seeking far more when it comes to paying up top dollar for these institutions. And even in these cases, the decision between primary, secondary and compounding capital is going to become more and more critical. So yes, its a theme to stay. We're seeing very high-quality names come through. But this theme is going to really become one in which institutions are going to ask for a lot more from the MNCs as well. Jibi Jacob: Just to add to that, from a market perspective also, especially from investors, there is a clear understanding of why MNC’s are coming here. And from an investor perspective, it's great if you have both of two specific variables. When I say two variables, one is the revenue and second is the cost. If you have both of that inbuilt into India, and there were a couple of issuances from MNC’s where both these variables were residing in in India, that’s good. If not, at least one of the variables must reside in India and that is how it becomes a bit of an India-centric issuance. Traditionally, for a few companies listed in India, in the pharma and IT space, the revenue stream is overseas, but the cost and the fulfillment are happening in India. So we are telling issuers that it's great to have both variables in India, if not at least one. There have been a couple of issuers, purely from the valuation perspective, trying to see if they can list in India. They just have one operating entity, but the cost and the revenue reside out. And in our view, that is something on which the buy-side investors will have far more deeper questions. If your revenue and cost doesn't reside here, then India is not your home market in a real sense. So, let's see how this market deepens from here on. But as long as one of the variables resides here, we will see this theme play out.
